topical.text: Ceramide-rich emollients BID · Topical steroid (potency matched to site) · Topical calcineurin inhibitors (tacrolimus 0.1%, pimecrolimus 1%) · Crisaborole (PDE4 inhibitor) · Ruxolitinib cream 1.5% (JAK1/2, age ≥12)
topical.detail: Emollients: Foundation of all AD therapy; apply within 3 minutes of bathing (soak-and-smear). Topical steroids: match potency to body site — avoid high-potency on face, axillae, groin. TCIs (tacrolimus/pimecrolimus): steroid-sparing for sensitive areas; FDA black-box (rare lymphoma risk historically debated). Crisaborole 2%: non-steroidal PDE4 inhibitor; effective for mild-moderate AD (age ≥2). Ruxolitinib cream: rapid itch relief (within 36h in trials); approved for mild-moderate AD age ≥12. PMID 23614588.

systemic-nonimmune.text: Sedating H1 antihistamines at bedtime (hydroxyzine, diphenhydramine) for sleep disruption · Non-sedating H1 (fexofenadine, cetirizine) — limited efficacy in AD
systemic-nonimmune.detail: Antihistamines have limited direct anti-pruritic efficacy in AD (itch is not primarily histamine-mediated in AD). Sedating antihistamines (hydroxyzine 25-50mg QHS) are used for sleep disruption only. Caution in elderly (anticholinergic effects, fall risk).

systemic-targeted.text: Select an age-appropriate, labeled AD therapy after evaluating severity, prior treatment, comorbidities, risk and preference. Biologics and oral JAK inhibitors are not interchangeable, and superiority of one itch endpoint does not establish an overall best therapy. Verify current labels rather than a 2013 general-itch citation.

topical.text: Cooling moisturizer / menthol-containing lotion (1% menthol in aqueous cream) · Lukewarm showers (avoid hot water) · Physical cooling vest for severe intractable itch
topical.detail: Cooling stimulates cold-sensitive TRPM8 receptors, inhibiting itch sensation at the peripheral level. Menthol 1% in emollient provides temporary relief of cholestatic itch and is well-tolerated. Avoid hot water — heat exacerbates bile acid-mediated itch. Physical cooling devices (ice packs, cooling vests) can dramatically reduce itch intensity in severe cholestatic pruritus.

systemic-nonimmune.text: Hepatology-directed options may include cholestyramine, rifampin, naltrexone or sertraline with individualized titration, interactions and monitoring. Do not transfer PBC treatment to ICP. Obeticholic acid is not an antipruritic recommendation.

systemic-targeted.text: Linerixibat (Lynavoy) is FDA-approved for PBC-associated cholestatic pruritus (March 17, 2026); use the current label. Other IBAT drugs have different pediatric disease indications. Severe refractory cholestatic itch may warrant transplant-center assessment in selected patients; it is not universally excluded as a consideration.

topical.text: Ceramide-containing emollients BID (reduce TEWL) · Capsaicin 0.025-0.075% cream (TRPV1 desensitization) · Pramoxine 1% lotion (topical anesthetic) · Tacrolimus 0.1% ointment (localized areas)
topical.detail: Emollients: Uremic patients have impaired barrier function + xerosis; ceramide-rich formulas preferred. Capsaicin: Depletes substance P from cutaneous nerve endings; initial burning sensation limits tolerability. Begin with 0.025% and titrate. High-concentration capsaicin 8% patch (Qutenza) may be useful under specialist supervision. Pramoxine: Available in specialized CKD pruritus formulations; well-tolerated.

systemic-nonimmune.text: Optimize dialysis and treat xerosis and other contributors. Consider off-label gabapentinoids only with an individualized renal/dialysis-adjusted regimen and monitoring for neurotoxicity, sedation and falls; pregabalin 25–75 mg twice daily is not a default dialysis prescription.

systemic-targeted.text: Difelikefalin 0.5 mcg/kg IV post-dialysis (κ-opioid receptor agonist) — FDA-approved 2021 · Nemolizumab (IL-31Rα) — investigational for CKD pruritus
systemic-targeted.detail: Difelikefalin (Korsuva): First FDA-approved therapy specifically for CKD-associated pruritus in hemodialysis adults. Peripherally restricted κ-opioid receptor agonist (does not cross BBB); administered IV 3×/week after dialysis. Significantly reduces Worst Itching Intensity NRS vs placebo in KALM-1 and KALM-2 trials. Does not require renal dose adjustment. Main side effects: dizziness, nausea, somnolence. PMID 23614588.

topical.text: Selected topical anesthetics or capsaicin can be considered. An 8% capsaicin patch is approved for particular neuropathic pain indications, not pruritus; neither its pain-label application time nor duration of benefit is automatically validated for itch.

systemic-nonimmune.text: Gabapentin 300-3600mg/day (titrate) · Pregabalin 75-300mg/day · Tricyclic antidepressants: amitriptyline 10-75mg QHS or nortriptyline · Duloxetine (SNRI) 60mg QD for SFN · Physical therapy / paraspinal muscle release (notalgia) · Cervical traction / surgery (brachioradial, structural cause)
systemic-nonimmune.detail: Gabapentinoids: First-line systemic for neuropathic itch; alpha-2-delta calcium channel subunit blockade reduces ectopic nerve firing. Titrate slowly; common side effects: dizziness, somnolence, weight gain. TCAs: Amitriptyline for sleep disruption + analgesic effect; nortriptyline better tolerated in elderly (less anticholinergic). Start 10mg QHS, titrate to 50-75mg. Duloxetine: SNRI with evidence in diabetic SFN. PMID 23614588.

systemic-targeted.text: Procedural therapies require a confirmed indication and specialist review. Botulinum-toxin evidence in notalgia paresthetica is limited and inconsistent; the listed sources do not justify a routine 50–100-unit regimen or a guaranteed 3–6-month benefit.

topical.text: Ceramide-rich emollients QD-BID (barrier restoration) · Menthol 1-2% (symptomatic cooling) · Topical calcineurin inhibitors off-label
topical.detail: In idiopathic chronic pruritus (diagnosis of exclusion), barrier restoration with emollients is the foundation. Menthol provides temporary relief. Topical steroids are generally not indicated in the absence of primary skin inflammation.

systemic-nonimmune.text: Gabapentin 300-1800mg/day · Pregabalin 75-150mg/day · Mirtazapine 15-30mg QHS (NK1 + H1 + NaSSA) · Doxepin 10-25mg QHS (potent H1/H2 antihistamine) · Aprepitant 80mg QD (NK1 receptor antagonist) · Low-dose naltrexone 1.5-4.5mg QHS
systemic-nonimmune.detail: Mirtazapine: NaSSA antidepressant; potent H1 and NK1 receptor antagonism; excellent for nocturnal pruritus; start 15mg QHS (weight gain, sedation are common side effects). Doxepin: Potent H1 + H2 + muscarinic antagonist at low doses; 10-25mg QHS; avoid in elderly (anticholinergic burden). Aprepitant: NK1 receptor antagonist (antiemetic drug); off-label; evidence in cancer-related, chronic renal, and idiopathic pruritus. Low-dose naltrexone: Emerging evidence in pruritus; immunomodulatory at 1.5-4.5mg (different mechanism from standard 50mg dose). PMID 23614588.

systemic-targeted.text: Nemolizumab (IL-31Rα mAb) — approved for prurigo nodularis (2023); emerging evidence in chronic pruritus · Dupilumab off-label if atopic background suspected · Aprepitant (NK1R) — used in cancer-related and chronic pruritus
systemic-targeted.detail: Nemolizumab: IL-31 receptor α-chain blocking antibody; IL-31 is a key pruritogen driving itch and prurigo nodularis. FDA-approved for prurigo nodularis (age ≥12) in 2023; off-label for idiopathic chronic itch. SQ Q4W. Dupilumab: Off-label for chronic pruritus without AD; may be effective when atopic background or type 2 inflammation suspected but not formally diagnosed. Caution: use evidence-based indications; document atopic features before prescribing. PMID 23614588.
